title: Train v. Colorado Public Interest Research Group (1976)
summary: Source, byproduct, and special nuclear materials regulated by the Atomic Energy Commission are not "pollutants" under the Federal Water Pollution Control Act, because the legislative history shows Congress meant to leave the Atomic Energy Act's scheme untouched even though the statutory definition says "radioactive materials" without qualification.
notes: Supreme Court of the United States, 1976. Key line: "To the extent that the Court of Appeals excluded reference to the legislative history of the FWPCA in discerning its meaning, the court was in error." (Justice Marshall)

sections.Parties: Petitioner is Russell Train, Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, who adopted permit regulations excluding from the FWPCA program the three categories of radioactive material regulated by the Atomic Energy Commission. Respondents are the Colorado Public Interest Research Group and other parties who argued that these materials are "pollutants" whose discharge into navigable waters requires an EPA or state permit, so that AEC licenses would have to conform to FWPCA permits. The dispute pits an agency's reading of its own enabling statute, based on legislative history, against a challenger's reliance on the unqualified words of the statutory definition. The Atomic Energy Commission and its successor, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, are the agencies whose exclusive authority was at stake.
sections.Material Facts: Since 1946 the federal government has controlled atomic energy through the AEC, and under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 private parties may produce atomic energy only under AEC licenses. The AEA scheme covers source, special nuclear, and byproduct material, and 42 U.S.C. section 2201(b) lets the AEC set standards to protect health and minimize danger to life or property. AEC regulations set maximum permissible releases and require effluents kept "as low as is reasonably achievable" (10 CFR sections 20.1(c) and 50.34a). The 1972 FWPCA amendments set a goal of eliminating discharges of "pollutants" by 1985, required "best practicable control technology" by July 1, 1977 and "best available technology" by July 1, 1983, and made discharges unlawful without an EPA or state permit. Section 1362(6) defines "pollutant" to include "radioactive materials." EPA's permit regulation, 40 CFR section 125.1(y) (1975), excluded AEA-regulated materials on the basis of legislative history, listing radium and accelerator-produced isotopes as the radioactive materials still covered.
sections.Procedural History: Respondents challenged EPA's exclusion of AEA-regulated materials from the FWPCA permit program. The Court of Appeals ruled for respondents, resolving the question exclusively by reference to the statutory language: the FWPCA defines "pollution" as alteration of the "radiological integrity of water," and the definition of "pollutant" lists "radioactive materials" without any express qualification or exception. The Supreme Court granted certiorari. Justice Marshall wrote for the Court, holding that the Court of Appeals erred to the extent it refused to consider legislative history, and reversed. Justice Stevens took no part in the consideration or decision of the case; no Justice dissented.
sections.Issue: Whether EPA has authority under the Federal Water Pollution Control Act, as amended in 1972, to regulate discharges of source, byproduct, and special nuclear materials that are already regulated by the Atomic Energy Commission under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954. In statutory terms, whether those materials are "pollutants" within 33 U.S.C. section 1362(6), which lists "radioactive materials" among the things a pollutant includes. A threshold methodological question is whether a court may consult legislative history when the words of the statute appear clear on their face, or whether the plain meaning of "radioactive materials" ends the inquiry.
sections.Holding: The "pollutants" subject to regulation under the FWPCA do not include source, byproduct, and special nuclear materials, and the EPA Administrator acted within his statutory mandate in declining to regulate their discharge. The Court of Appeals erred in excluding legislative history; when aids to construction are available there is no rule of law forbidding their use, however clear the words appear on superficial examination. The House Committee Report, the Senate colloquy between Senators Pastore and Muskie, the House's 3-to-1 rejection of the Wolff amendment, and Representative Harsha's explanation of the Conference Report all show that Congress intended to preserve the AEC's exclusive scheme. Judgment reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Marshall used legislative history to read "radioactive materials" more narrowly than its literal scope, citing American Trucking for the rule that aids to construction may be used however clear the words appear. Four pieces of history carried the case. First, House Report 92-911 said "radioactive materials" means those not covered by the AEA, naming radium and accelerator-produced isotopes as examples. Second, Senator Muskie, the Act's primary author, assured Senator Pastore, Chairman of the Joint Committee on Atomic Energy, that the bill did not affect the AEC's powers or alter Northern States Power v. Minnesota, which held that the AEA preempts state regulation of radioactive effluents. Third, the House defeated by 3 to 1 the Wolff amendment, which would have let states regulate nuclear plant discharges; opponents relied on the committee report, and the amendment would have been superfluous if the materials were already pollutants. Fourth, Representative Harsha told the House the conference report kept that intent. Marshall also harmonized statutes: bringing these materials under the FWPCA, with its state permit programs and stricter state limits, would significantly alter the AEA's pervasive scheme, and the Court expected a clear indication of intent before finding such a change. No Justice dissented; the contrary view was the Court of Appeals' plain-meaning approach, which respondents defended.

topics.lrs-k-legislative-history: The Court relies on a committee report, a floor colloquy between the Act's author and a committee chairman, a rejected floor amendment, and a conference manager's statement, ranking each as evidence of what Congress meant.
topics.lrs-k-purposivism: Marshall treats the question as what Congress intended for AEC-regulated materials, and lets that intent control over the literal breadth of "radioactive materials."
topics.lrs-k-textualism: The Court of Appeals' plain-meaning ruling is the foil: the unqualified words of section 1362(6) would cover all radioactive materials, and the Court says that reading contributes little once the history is consulted.
topics.lrs-k-implied-repeal: The Court expects a clear indication of legislative intent before reading the FWPCA to alter the AEA's pervasive regulatory scheme, so the later statute is not read to displace the earlier one.
topics.lrs-k-statutory-structure: The FWPCA's state permit programs and stricter state limits are contrasted with the AEA's exclusive federal control to show that the two schemes were not meant to overlap.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Marshall wrote for a unanimous Court of eight; Justice Stevens took no part in the consideration or decision. There were no concurrences or dissents in the excerpt.
learning.why: Train is the standard example of the older, purposive approach in which a court consults committee reports, floor colloquies, rejected amendments, and conference explanations to override apparently plain words, and it supplies the American Trucking line that textualists later attack. It also shows a court reading a new statute so as not to disturb an existing comprehensive regulatory scheme.
